title: India Scrapped Taxes on Its Bonds. $3.4 Billion Poured In Within Weeks.
excerpt: New Delhi's most aggressive capital-market reform in years has unlocked record foreign inflows, and Bloomberg's biggest bond index could be next.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India's bond tax reforms attracted $3.4 billion in foreign investments within weeks.
  • The removal of taxes makes Indian bonds more appealing to global investors.
  • Bloomberg may soon include India in its Global Aggregate Bond Index.
  • Foreign investors bought ₹29,900 crore ($3.16 billion) of bonds in June alone.
  • Falling oil prices and tax reforms have led to a decline in bond yields.

When India scrapped taxes on government bonds for foreign investors on June 5, the response was immediate — and historic. In less than four weeks, overseas institutions poured a record $3.4 billion into Indian sovereign debt, more than double the $1.7 billion that had trickled in over the previous five months combined. The reform, engineered jointly by the Finance Ministry and the Reserve Bank of India, eliminated the 12.5 per cent long-term capital gains tax and the 20 per cent withholding tax on bond interest income for foreign portfolio investors. The RBI simultaneously broadened the pool of securities under its Fully Accessible Route — the channel through which overseas investors can buy Indian government bonds without investment caps — to include longer-dated sovereign debt. ## The Bloomberg Question The numbers are striking on their own. But the bigger prize — and the reason global bond desks are paying attention — is what these reforms might unlock next: India's potential inclusion in the Bloomberg Global Aggregate Bond Index, one of the most widely tracked fixed-income benchmarks in the world. Market participants now expect Bloomberg Index Services to announce its decision this month. A senior portfolio manager at BNP Paribas Asset Management described the reforms as addressing the biggest remaining roadblocks — particularly the tax issue, which had left India out of step with other zero-tax sovereign issuers already in the index. "The removal of taxation on Indian government bonds will mechanically make them more interesting for global investors," said Niel Clement, a portfolio manager for emerging market fixed income at BNP Paribas. "Liquidity and market depth have also now been improved, as this benchmark requires a deep pool of investable assets." Jennifer Taylor, head of emerging market debt at State Street Investment Management — which manages about $5.6 trillion — went further, calling the changes "a game-changer for debt flows" and saying Bloomberg index inclusion now appears to be on the horizon. ## What Changed — and Why India's bond market has long been a curiosity for global investors: large, liquid enough at the top end, but walled off by taxes and restrictions that made it uncompetitive with peers. At a time when emerging-market bond allocations were already under pressure — from rising US Treasury yields, a strong dollar, and the Iran-linked oil shock — India's barriers made it easy to skip. The June 5 measures were a direct response to that calculus. New Delhi had watched the rupee slide to record lows near 97 per dollar in May, pushed by sustained foreign selling of Indian assets and high energy costs. The bond-tax reforms were part of a broader salvo that included incentives for banks to raise foreign currency deposits from NRIs and easier overseas borrowing for Indian companies. The result has been a sharp reversal. Foreign investors bought a net ₹29,900 crore ($3.16 billion) of FAR bonds in June alone, according to clearing house data. Goldman Sachs now projects foreign flows into Indian government bonds will reach $10 billion for the full year, a figure that would have seemed unlikely six months ago. ## Yields Have Already Moved The 10-year benchmark bond yield has fallen 28 basis points over the past five weeks to around 6.72 per cent — its fifth consecutive weekly decline. Shorter maturities have seen even larger drops. Indian bonds shrugged off a selloff in US Treasuries this week, with traders citing sustained foreign demand and Bloomberg index expectations as the key supports. Falling oil prices have amplified the rally. Brent crude has retreated over 20 per cent from its quarter highs to around $70 per barrel, easing inflation fears for oil-dependent India and giving the RBI room to keep its accommodative stance.

## The NRI and Diaspora Connection For Indians abroad, the reforms carry direct implications. The tax exemptions apply specifically to foreign portfolio investors — a category that includes many funds and structures through which NRIs access Indian capital markets. A deeper, more liquid government bond market with institutional foreign participation could also stabilise the rupee over time, protecting the value of remittances and India-linked investments. If Bloomberg index inclusion materialises, the effect would be structural: funds that track the Global Aggregate would be required to hold Indian bonds, creating a steady, passive demand floor that India's debt market has never had. RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra, speaking at an event in Russia this week, reinforced the positive macro backdrop, saying India is unlikely to raise its official inflation target and that there may be a case for lowering it over the long term. ## What Comes Next The momentum is real, but not without caveats. Elevated US interest rates continue to push the dollar higher, and the Iran-linked uncertainty in the Gulf has not fully resolved — oil prices remain sensitive to any breakdown in the interim peace deal. India's Finance Ministry is scheduled to sell ₹34,000 crore of the 10-year note on Friday, a test of whether foreign demand can absorb large supply. And Bloomberg's index decision, whenever it comes, will hinge not just on the tax reforms but on operational factors like settlement efficiency and capital repatriation — areas where India has improved but still trails some peers. Still, for a market that was being largely ignored by global allocators as recently as April, the turnaround has been remarkable. India didn't just open its bond market — it made it competitive. The world has noticed.
